doc.title: Ray Ricker interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 27, 2022

title: Avoiding sounding the same: broad listening and Cannonball
summary: Responding to Sweets Edison's remark, Ricker urges students to forge their own sound and listen widely; Rowe and Ricker name Cannonball and Getz.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Before I forget, I was looking at the course listing at Eastman for a four year degree and it reminded me of something Harry “Sweets” Edison said. I’m paraphrasing a little bit, nowadays it seems like musicians have their idols and they don’t venture anyplace else. It’s better to be the world’s worst originator than the world’s greatest imitator. So my question I guess is, because jazz playing, improvising, has been so codified and so much © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-
information the people from Sweets’ generation over and over said everybody sounds the same. How do you think players can avoid that?

Yeah, I think it’s something you can’t force you know. And you know if everybody is more or less doing, practicing the same stuff that’s going to — I mean you get out what’s put in and if you all are more or less inputting the same stuff through you, you know, the same play-a-long records, you know, that’s how — well I mean it happens in America. I mean we can go into certain — we could be in Idaho someplace and go into a shopping mall and see the same stores there as we have here. So that’s happening that way too. But I think what you do is have to forge your own, take your own background and experience and make that into something that’s you. And that means being — I tell students — okay you’re here at Eastman don’t just have it be jazz, jazz, jazz all day. Know that there’s world class singers that you can hear, you could hear — you know go to an opera, go to an orchestra concert, go to the new music people, go to the gamelan and check that stuff out. You know, you have to know — the, you know you have some scholarly kind of series that they have at school. And try to — I had one guy that was so really good, really into Cannonball and was just Cannonball, Cannonball, Cannonball. And I finally said, you’ve got to turn the page. You can’t stay on this all the time. You know? You got it, go on to the next thing.

I’m cracking up because if you look over my shoulder, I don’t know if you can tell but that’s Cannonball Adderley and he’s been my guy. And I saw him actually in Rochester a number of times. I mean it’s not the only person I listen to but for me he had everything I wanted from a saxophone player.
Yeah. Well there’s nothing wrong with that. Stan Getz was my guy you know.
